introduction: These readings treat happiness as a spiritual condition and a duty. They distinguish a physical happiness that passes from a spiritual one that does not; they tell of joy kept in exile and prison; they prescribe joy as medicine, proclaim the present as a day of rejoicing, and ask believers to wear a cheerful face and to make others glad. A hundred of the guide's hundred and fifty-nine quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Four in five stand alongside: the Psalms' fulness of joy, Paul rejoicing in chains, Habakkuk's 'yet I will rejoice', Confucius content with coarse rice, the merry heart of Proverbs, Lovelace's stone walls, the Dhammapada's 'let us live happily'. A fifth push back or add a side: Ecclesiastes preferring the house of mourning, Jesus 'exceeding sorrowful', Arnold's joyless world, the Qur'an's 'exult not', Mill's finding that happiness asked after is lost, Keats and Blake on joy that cannot be held, and Paul's 'weep with them that weep'.
questions: The readings divide happiness into a physical kind that ends and a spiritual kind that does not. Where do you recognize each in your own experience?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of joy in forty years of prison; Paul sings in jail; Confucius is glad with coarse rice. What do such accounts have in common, and what do they not claim?
'You must always be happy.' Mill found that asking whether one is happy ends it. Can joy be commanded, and what would obeying look like?
Ecclesiastes prefers the house of mourning, and Jesus was 'exceeding sorrowful'. What place do the readings leave for grief?
A cheerful face is asked for the sake of others. When does it comfort, and when should one 'weep with them that weep'?
The readings say the best cure is joy. What in your day could be given to causing happiness?

outside.why: Proverbs observes that heaviness in the heart makes it stoop, but a good word makes it glad.
Paul recalls a saying of Jesus found nowhere else: it is more blessed to give than to receive.
Ecclesiastes finds no good but to rejoice and do good, and to enjoy the fruit of one's labour as the gift of God.
Proverbs calls happy the man who finds wisdom, whose gain is better than silver or fine gold.
The American Declaration counts the pursuit of happiness among the rights of all. Is happiness something pursued, or the fruit of something else?
Ecclesiastes joins the two kinds of gladness: eat thy bread with joy, and let thy garments be always white.
A psalm has the same assurance: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Jesus told his disciples that they would weep and lament, but that their sorrow would be turned into joy.
A psalm places joy where the reading does: in thy presence is fulness of joy, at thy right hand pleasures for evermore.
The angel in Luke hails the shepherds with good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
Mill too ranks pleasures: better a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
Whitman thought he could turn and live with animals, so placid and self-contained, who do not whine about their condition. Is animal contentment as low as the reading says?
A psalm knows a gladness of heart greater than that of the season when corn and wine increased.
Blake asks how the bird that is born for joy can sit in a cage and sing.
Ecclesiastes says that sorrow is better than laughter, for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. Is life made for happiness alone?
Mencius held that all things are already complete in us, and that there is no greater delight than to find oneself sincere.
The Qur'an says that it is in the remembrance of God that hearts find rest.
Augustine says the same to God: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
Pascal traced all human unhappiness to one fact, that people cannot stay quietly in their own chamber. What is it we run from?
Jesus advised laying up treasure where moth and rust do not corrupt, for where the treasure is, the heart will be.
Hebrews says that Jesus endured the cross for the joy that was set before him.
Peter writes of those who, believing without having seen, rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
Jesus tells his disciples he has spoken so that his joy might remain in them and their joy be full.
The Preacher tried mirth and pleasure and judged them vanity: of laughter he said, it is mad.
Keats finds that in the very temple of Delight veiled Melancholy has her shrine. Is passing joy an illusion, or only inseparable from its ending?
Blake says that whoever binds a joy to himself destroys it, while whoever kisses it as it flies lives in eternity's sunrise. Is that another way of loosening one's hold on this world?
A psalmist would go to the altar of God, 'unto God my exceeding joy', and praise him on the harp.
Paul says the kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
Lovelace held that stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage, for one whose soul is free.
In Acts, Paul and Silas pray and sing praises to God at midnight, and the prisoners hear them.
Paul describes the apostles as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
Habakkuk says that though the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield no food, yet he will rejoice in the Lord.
Confucius said that with coarse rice, water to drink and his bent arm for a pillow, he still had joy.
Proverbs says that he who is of a merry heart has a continual feast.
Paul says that he has learned, in whatever state he is, therewith to be content.
Milton has a speaker claim that the mind is its own place and can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven.
Paul's rule is short: rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, in every thing give thanks.
James tells his readers to count it all joy when they fall into trials, since the trying of faith works patience.
Marcus Aurelius would be like the promontory on which waves break, saying not 'unhappy am I' but 'happy am I, though this has happened'.
Jesus told his disciples: blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
Mill found that to ask yourself whether you are happy is to cease to be so, and that happiness comes by aiming at something else. Can anyone be happy by command?
Proverbs has the same medicine: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine, but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Macbeth asks a physician whether he can minister to a mind diseased and pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow. What can reach where medicine cannot?
Paul says God has not left himself without witness, sending rain and fruitful seasons and filling our hearts with food and gladness.
Paul's instruction to the Philippians is the same: rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice.
Thoreau agreed about the world as it is: the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
Jesus invites those who labour and are heavy laden to come to him and find rest for their souls.
Jesus told his friends that his soul was exceeding sorrowful, even unto death, and asked them to watch with him. Is grief a failure, or sometimes the truth of the hour?
Shakespeare has a character urge: give sorrow words, for the grief that does not speak bids the heart break. When is silence about suffering wise, and when harmful?
Longfellow says our destined end is neither enjoyment nor sorrow, but to act so that each tomorrow finds us farther. Is happiness the aim, or a by-product?
Nehemiah told the people not to be sorry but to feast and send portions to those with nothing, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
Isaiah sees the ransomed return with everlasting joy upon their heads, and sorrow and sighing flee away.
The first believers in Acts broke bread from house to house and ate with gladness and singleness of heart.
A psalm says: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
Isaiah promises those who mourn in Zion beauty for ashes, and the oil of joy for mourning.
A psalm calls all things to rejoice: let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad.
Arnold wrote that the world, which seems so various and beautiful, has really neither joy, nor love, nor light. What would each side say to the other?
Isaiah pictures the mountains breaking into singing and the trees of the field clapping their hands.
The Song of Songs announces the same season: the winter is past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers appear.
A psalmist says to God: thou hast turned my mourning into dancing, and girded me with gladness.
The Dhammapada asks how there can be laughter and joy while this world is always burning. Is cheerfulness an answer to that, or an evasion of it?
The Dhammapada too exhorts: let us live happily, not hating those who hate us, free from hatred among the hating.
Ecclesiastes allows each its season: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Is there a right time for tears?
Zephaniah tells Zion that the Lord in her midst will rejoice over her with joy and rest in his love.
The elder writes that he has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in truth.
The priestly blessing asks that the Lord bless and keep thee, and make his face shine upon thee.
Paul says the apostles do not lord it over the faith of the Corinthians, but are helpers of their joy.
Paul thanks God at every remembrance of his friends at Philippi, and prays for them with joy.
A psalm promises: delight thyself in the Lord, and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
Jesus tells his disciples to ask, and they shall receive, that their joy may be full.
A psalm summons the people: O come, let us sing unto the Lord, let us make a joyful noise.
In the Qur'an Korah's people tell him: exult not, for God loveth not the exultant. How is spiritual gladness told apart from exulting?
A psalm of return remembers: then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.
Proverbs notes that even in laughter the heart is sorrowful, and the end of that mirth is heaviness. Can joy be shown that is not felt?
The Qur'an says: in the bounty of God and in his mercy, therein let them rejoice.
James gives the plain rule: is any afflicted, let him pray; is any merry, let him sing psalms.
Paul's list for the Romans joins the two: rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation.
Jesus told the returning disciples to rejoice not in their powers but because their names are written in heaven.
Proverbs warns: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth. How should the joy of the faithful regard those who wished them ill?
Confucius asks: is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
The man in the parable who finds treasure hidden in a field goes, for joy of it, and sells all that he has.
Proverbs says that a merry heart makes a cheerful countenance, but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
Stevenson's child thinks the world so full of a number of things that we should all be as happy as kings.
Paul asks for both: rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep. When does a cheerful face fail someone who grieves?
Jesus told those who fast not to put on a sad countenance as the hypocrites do.
The Qur'an says of the righteous that God has made them find brightness and joy.
Bacon says that opening oneself to a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in halves.
Ecclesiastes holds it better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. In a world like the one the reading describes, is there a place for sorrow?
Tennyson's new-year bells are heralds too: ring, happy bells, ring out the false, ring in the true.
Tagore says deliverance is not for him in renunciation: he feels the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight.
A psalm says that they that sow in tears shall reap in joy, and come again bringing their sheaves.
Jesus told his disciples the same: if ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.
The Ethics of the Fathers asks who is rich, and answers: he who rejoices in his lot.
Peter, seeing the great catch of fish, fell at Jesus' knees and said: depart from me, for I am a sinful man.
A psalm asks all lands to serve the Lord with gladness and come before his presence with singing.
Hebrews counsels: be content with such things as ye have, for he hath said, I will never leave thee.
The Qur'an describes those slain in the way of God as jubilant because of what he has bestowed on them.
Peter tells the persecuted not to think the fiery trial strange, but to rejoice as partakers of Christ's sufferings.
Deuteronomy makes joy a commandment of the calendar: thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, with thy household and the stranger.
A psalm ends in the same words: happy is that people whose God is the Lord.

proverbs-merry-heart-cheerful-countenanc.text: A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken

luke-ye-shall-laugh.text: Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh

isaiah-sorrow-and-sighing-shall-flee.text: And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away

psalm-serve-the-lord-with-gladness.text: Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all ye lands. Serve the Lord with gladness: come before his presence with singing

psalm-gladness-in-my-heart.text: Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased

proverbs-in-laughter-the-heart-is-sorrow.text: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness

proverbs-happy-is-the-man-that-findeth-w.text: Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding. For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold

psalm-happy-is-that-people.text: Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the Lord

psalm-mourning-into-dancing.text: Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness

ecclesiastes-rejoice-and-do-good.text: I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life. And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God

ecclesiastes-of-laughter-it-is-mad.text: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity. I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it

matthew-exceeding-great-joy.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy

proverbs-trusteth-in-the-lord-happy.text: He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he

psalm-god-my-exceeding-joy.text: Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God

ecclesiastes-time-to-weep-and-laugh.text: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance

isaiah-garments-of-salvation.text: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels

quran-exult-not.text: Now Korah was of Moses' folk, but he oppressed them; and We gave him so much treasure that the stores thereof would verily have been a burden for a troop of mighty men. When his own folk said unto him: Exult not; lo! Allah loveth not the exultant;

quran-brightness-and-joy.text: Therefor Allah hath warded off from them the evil of that day, and hath made them find brightness and joy;

quran-jubilant-martyrs.text: Jubilant (are they) because of that which Allah hath bestowed upon them of His bounty, rejoicing for the sake of those who have not joined them but are left behind: That there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve.

stevenson-happy-as-kings.text: world is so full of a number of things, / I'm sure we should all be as happy as kings
stevenson-happy-as-kings.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

blake-kisses-the-joy-as-it-flies.text: He who binds to himself a joy / Does the winged life destroy / But he who kisses the joy as it flies / Lives in eternity's sun rise
blake-kisses-the-joy-as-it-flies.author: William Blake

dhammapada-let-us-live-happily.text: Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred

keats-temple-of-delight.text: Ay, in the very temple of Delight / Veil'd Melancholy has her sovran shrine
keats-temple-of-delight.author: John Keats

wordsworth-bliss-of-solitude.text: For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude; / And then my heart with pleasure fills, / And dances with the daffodils
wordsworth-bliss-of-solitude.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-bliss-of-solitude.work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

mill-ask-yourself-whether-you-are-happy.text: Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so. The only chance is to treat, not happiness, but some end external to it, as the purpose of life
mill-ask-yourself-whether-you-are-happy.author: John Stuart Mill

corinthians-helpers-of-your-joy.text: Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand

philippians-request-with-joy.text: I thank my God upon every remembrance of you, Always in every prayer of mine for you all making request with joy

psalm-desires-of-thine-heart.text: Delight thyself also in the Lord: and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart
